content: The updated WHO guidelines for HIV patient monitoring and care include several new elements to enhance the tracking and management of individuals living with HIV. These updates focus on improving data collection, patient care, and program outcomes. Below is a detailed explanation of the key updates and definitions: 1. Monitoring Advanced HIV Disease: New data elements have been added to track advanced HIV disease, including the WHO functional status to assess the physical functionality of individuals with advanced HIV. 2. Immunization Updates: Childhood immunizations have been incorporated, and updates have been made to adult immunization records. 3. Developmental Disorders in Children: Data elements have been introduced to monitor developmental disorders in children. 4. 5. Adherence Counseling for Advanced HIV: Tailored adherence counseling for individuals with advanced HIV disease and enhanced counseling for those with unsuppressed viral loads have been added to the monitoring framework. 6. Rapid ART Initiation: The guidelines emphasize the importance of initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) within seven days of an HIV-positive diagnosis. If same-day initiation is not possible, prompt ART initiation is recommended once the patient is ready. 7. Definitions for Key Terms: Newly Enrolled in HIV Care: Refers to individuals with a confirmed HIV diagnosis who are registered for care at a facility or community ART site for the first time. This includes treatment-experienced patients without prior records or those who received ART from external sources. Retention in Care: Describes individuals actively receiving routine HIV care and ART at a specific time point, excluding those who have died or are lost to follow-up (LTFU). Transfer In: Refers to patients transferring their HIV care from one facility to another within the same system, with records or knowledge of their ART regimen and start date. Lost to Follow-Up (LTFU): Patients who have not been seen at a facility or community ART site for 28 days or more since their last missed appointment. Efforts should be made to contact these patients promptly. 8. HIV Patient Card Updates: The HIV patient card now includes fields for monitoring rapid ART initiation, eligibility for differentiated service delivery (DSD) models, and tracking tracing interventions for disengaged patients. Psychosocial interventions for adolescents and young adults, as well as tailored adherence support for individuals with advanced HIV disease, are also recorded. 9. ART Register Enhancements: The ART register has been updated to include new drug regimen codes, tracking of DSD enrollment, and monitoring of treatment-limiting toxicities such as weight gain. It also includes a column for tracking fluconazole prophylaxis for individuals with advanced HIV disease. 10. Cross-Sectional and Cohort Reports: Cross-sectional reports provide a snapshot of patient status at a specific time, including the number of individuals on ART and their treatment regimens. Cohort analysis reports track patient outcomes over time, such as retention, viral suppression, and mortality rates, allowing for trend analysis and program improvement. 11. Community ART Services: 12. Data Collection Tools: Standardized tools, such as the HIV patient card and ART register, are recommended for tracking patient care and outcomes. These tools facilitate longitudinal monitoring of patients and aggregation of data for program evaluation. 13. Integration with Other Services: The guidelines emphasize the integration of HIV care with maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) and tuberculosis (TB) services, ensuring comprehensive care and data reconciliation. 14. Electronic Medical Records (EMRs): Where available, EMRs should be used to streamline data entry and improve the accuracy of patient monitoring. 15. Focus on Person-Centered Care: The guidelines prioritize person-centered approaches, ensuring that care is tailored to individual needs and that data collection supports actionable insights for improving outcomes. These updates aim to strengthen HIV care delivery, improve patient outcomes, and enhance the quality and use of data for program monitoring and decision-making.
